You are correct, but it wasn't just corporations who knew, but science in general. With that said, more research is needed. Are you ready for some science? Soybean, and the majority of seed oils are rich in 18-carbon omega-6 fats. These fats are the precursors of a 20-carbon omega-6 fat called arachidonic acid (ARA), which in turn is the precursor to tons of extremely important signaling molecules in your body. ARA is converted to prostaglandins and leukotrienes by the action of cyclooxygenase and lipoxygenase respectively. These are inflammation and immune modulation molecules. ARA is also converted to anandamide which is the molecule which signals your brain that you are hungry (fun fact, anandamide's target receptor is the same one THC binds to which makes you get the munchies). It is reasonable to hypothesize that omega-6 rich diets will promote inflammation and overeating, and from that, obesity and diabetes (but this is one area which needs more direct testing).

With that said, it has been known for a very long time that the rise of metabolic syndrome in the west is linked with pro-inflammatory reactions rooted in our western diets which are strongly biased towards omega-6 fats. It is also known that diets which are rich in saturated fats blow up your cholesterol levels, (but in order to have a heart attack, you also need inflammation). We used to think that eating more polyunsaturated fats (like soybean oil) would be healthier than saturates (like butter and coconut oil) because the polys don't raise your cholesterol as much, and thus the USDA focused more resources and incentives into polyunsaturated oilseed crops (like soybean). Those assumptions were bolstered by the fact that Japanese people which have much lower heart disease rates ate lots of soybean oil too.

What we've learned since is that it also matters which polyunsaturaed fats you are eating. The Japanese also eat a ton of fish too, which is high in omega-3 fats (which are anti-inflammatory, and also do not promote cholesterol), and the Japanese have some of the highest serum omega-3/omega-6 ratios in the world. Westerners have the lowest. However, westerners still eat too little fish and the best agricultural crop for omega-3 oils (flaxseed) is not as scalable as soybean. This has led several scientists to engineer healthy omega-3 fish oils into some of the more prominent seed oils, so that we can continue to exploit the economies of scale and the infrastructure around the big oilseed crops, while making those oils healthier, and hopefully reducing metabolic syndrome in western diets.
